column2: On the authority of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace), the truthful one, the one believed, narrated to us:

“The creation of each one of you is gathered in his mother's womb for forty days as a drop (nuṭfah), then he becomes a clinging clot (ʿalaqah) for a like period, then a lump of flesh (muḍghah) for a like period. Then the angel is sent to him, breathes the soul into him, and is commanded with four words:

to write down his provision, his lifespan, his deeds, and whether he will be wretched or happy. By Allah, besides whom there is no god, one of you will do the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is only a forearm's length between him and it,

then what is written overtakes him, and he does the deeds of the people of the Fire and enters it. And one of you will do the deeds of the people of the Fire until there is only a forearm's length between him and it, then what is written overtakes him, and he does the deeds of the people of Paradise and enters it.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
His words, “the truthful one, the one believed”, mean truthful in what he says and believed in the revelation he brought. Ibn Masʿūd said this only
because the hadith concerns matters of the unseen that can be known only through revelation.

His words, “The creation of each one of you is gathered in his mother's womb”: it has been said that the man's fluid is gathered together with the woman's fluid in the womb, and the human being is created from them, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “He was created from a fluid, ejected” [al-Ṭāriq 86:6], and He said:

“Did We not create you from a despised fluid, and place it in a firm lodging?” [al-Mursalāt 77:20–21]. What is meant by “his creation” is that from which the human being is created; it has come in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (1438): “The child does not come from all of the fluid.”

This hadith mentions the stages of the creation of the human being: first, the drop (nuṭfah), which is a small amount of fluid; second, the clinging clot (ʿalaqah), which is thick, congealed blood; and third, the lump of flesh (muḍghah), which is a piece of flesh the size of what one chews. Allah mentioned these three in His words:

“O mankind, if you are in doubt about the resurrection, then [know that] We created you from dust, then from a drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed” [al-Ḥajj 22:5]. The meaning of “formed and unformed” is shaped and unshaped.
The passage that sets out the stages of human creation most fully is the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in Sūrat al-Muʾminūn:

“And We certainly created man from an extract of clay; then We placed him as a drop in a firm lodging; then We made the drop into a clinging clot, and We made the clot into a lump of flesh, and We made the lump into bones, and We clothed the bones with flesh; then We brought him forth as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators” [al-Muʾminūn 23:12–14].
The hadith shows that after these three stages have passed, a period of one hundred and twenty days, the soul is breathed into him and he becomes a living human being;
before that he is dead. It has come in the Noble Qurʾān that the human being has two lives and two deaths, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said of the disbelievers:

“They will say: Our Lord, You caused us to die twice and gave us life twice” [Ghāfir 40:11]. The first death is what precedes the breathing in of the soul; the first life is from the breathing in of the soul until the end of the appointed term; the second death is from after death until the resurrection—and this death does not contradict the life of the barzakh, which is established by the Book and the Sunnah—

and the second life is the life after the resurrection, which is everlasting and continues without end. Allah made clear these four states of the human being in His words: “And it is He who gave you life, then causes you to die, then will give you life. Indeed, man is ungrateful” [al-Ḥajj 22:66], and His words:

“How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die, then He will give you life, then to Him you will be returned?” [al-Baqarah 2:28]. If, after the soul has been breathed into him, he is born dead, the rulings of birth apply to him:

he is washed and prayed over, the waiting period (ʿiddah) [of his mother] ends, a slave-woman [who bore him] becomes an umm walad, and his mother is in postnatal bleeding (nifās). If he is miscarried before that, these rulings do not apply to him.

Once the angel has written down his provision, his lifespan, whether male or female, and whether wretched or happy, knowledge of whether [the child] is male or female is not part of the knowledge of the unseen that is exclusive to Allah the Exalted,
because the angel has come to know it; so it is possible to know whether the foetus is male or female.
Allah's decree has preceded everything that will be, and what counts for happiness or wretchedness is the state a person is in at death.
People's states with respect to beginnings and endings are four:
First: one whose beginning is good and whose ending is good.
Second: one whose beginning is bad and whose ending is bad.
Third: one whose beginning is good and whose ending is bad, like someone who grew up obeying Allah, but before death apostatised from Islam and died in apostasy.

Fourth: one whose beginning is bad and whose ending is good, like Pharaoh's sorcerers who believed in the Lord of Hārūn and Mūsā, and like the Jewish boy who used to serve the Prophet ﷺ, whom the Prophet ﷺ visited in his illness;
he invited him to Islam and he accepted Islam, and the Prophet ﷺ said: “Praise be to Allah, who saved him from the Fire.” It is in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (1356).
This hadith indicates the last two states.

The hadith shows that a person does the deeds that bring about his happiness or wretchedness by his own will and choice, yet in doing so he does not go outside the will and wish of Allah. He has free choice in that he acts by his own choosing,

and he is directed in that nothing comes from him that Allah has not willed. Both matters are indicated by what is in this hadith, that before death what is written overtakes him, and he does the deeds of the people of Paradise or the deeds of the people of the Fire.
A person must live between fear and hope,
because some people do good in their lives and then their lives are sealed with a bad ending; and he should not cut himself off from hope,
for a person may commit sins for a long time, and then Allah favours him with guidance, and he is guided at the end of his life.

Al-Nawawī said in his explanation of this hadith: “If it is said: Allah the Exalted has said: ‘Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds—indeed, We will not allow to be lost the reward of anyone who did well in deeds’ [al-Kahf 18:30];

the apparent meaning of the verse is that the righteous deed of a sincere person is accepted, and once acceptance is secured by the promise of the Most Generous, he is thereby safe from a bad ending. The answer is from two angles:

First, that this is conditional on the conditions of acceptance and of a good ending being met; and it may be that whoever believes and makes his deeds sincere will always have his life sealed with nothing but good.

Second, that a bad ending happens only to someone whose deeds were bad, or who mixed them with righteous deeds tainted with some showing off and seeking of reputation. This is indicated by the other hadith:

‘One of you will do the deeds of the people of Paradise, as it appears to people’, meaning as far as they can see, in improving his outward appearance while his inner self is corrupt and foul. And Allah the Exalted knows best.”
An explanation of the stages of human creation in the mother's womb.
The breathing in of the soul happens after one hundred and twenty days, and he thereby becomes a human being.
Among the angels are some entrusted with the wombs.
Belief in the unseen.
Belief in the decree, and that it has preceded everything that will be.
Swearing an oath without being asked to, in order to emphasise what one says.
Deeds are judged by their endings.
Combining fear and hope: whoever does good should fear a bad ending, and whoever does wrong should not despair of Allah's mercy.
Deeds are the cause of entering Paradise or the Fire.
Whoever has been written as wretched, his state is not known in this world, and likewise the reverse.
